items.text:
Three weeks ago, I wrote that Fable gives us the same diff as Opus and costs about five times more.
This week Anthropic made that post wrong, and I'm happy about it.

The new Opus and Fable prices landed, so I opened our model catalog to copy them into MadBench.
Screenshot attached; the annotations are mine.
I expected the usual small change and a slightly bigger invoice.
The input and output rows did move a little, which is roughly what I expected.
What I didn't expect was the cached read row, which dropped on both models, and on Fable it dropped hard.

"Why do you care about the cache row, Jack?", you'll ask me.
Because that row is most of what a coding agent costs us.

In a chat, you type a question and the model reads it once.
An agent in Magus and other agents works differently.
On every turn, it sends the whole conversation again, the system prompt, the CLAUDE.md, every file it opened, and every tool result so far.

The model reads the same files over and over, and a cached read is the price of each reread.

Like a contractor who rereads the whole brief every morning and bills you for the hour.
On our invoices at MadAppGang, the cache already saves 20 to 40%, and in a long Magus session most of the tokens are rereads.

So the five times in my Fable post came from the old cache price.
I don't know the new gap yet.

We're running the same tasks through MadBench again this week, and I'll post both invoices.

I have no idea how they did it.

My read is that a drop like this takes months of inference work, and this release it got the same effort as making the model smarter.

That deserves a thank you, so here it is.

#AI #opus5.5 #claudecode

Turning a long video into useful clips is still too manual. This repo automates the first pass.

AutoClip is an AI video clipping system for builders who want to turn YouTube, Bilibili, or local videos into highlight clips and collections.

It helps you move from a source video to editable outputs by extracting an outline, identifying topic time ranges, scoring segments, and generating clips.

Key features:

• Flexible video inputs – download from YouTube or Bilibili, or upload a local video file
• Model-provider choice – supports hosted providers plus local Ollama and LM Studio models
• Automated clip pipeline – analyzes content, identifies topic ranges, scores segments, and generates clip titles
• CLI and MCP support – run the tool from the command line or expose it as an MCP server for Cursor or Claude
• Progress visibility – uses asynchronous tasks with WebSocket progress updates

It’s open-source (MIT license).

items.text:
A big reason why people have been under the impression that TPUs or more generally “systolic array” architectures lag behind Nvidia GPUs for inference is because they notoriously struggled with running MoEs at first, while Nvidia’s SMs were an easier fit for small, dynamically shaped per expert matmuls  that are a characteristic of MoEs.

TPUs prefer static, compile time known in advance shapes, with dimensions that are multiples of the MXU size (128x128 or 256x256), and when you design your model you design with that in mind. You might sacrifice some albeit small amounts of flexibility (other ways around it) but the benefit is much higher op reuse and higher utilization on large GEMMs than GPUs. You also avoid register file access, shared memory access and the control overhead of GPUs because your weights stationary and the same data flow runs every time, you just load it fire and wait for the result. 

Ofc Google has since fixed MoE routing on TPUs with XLA & custom kernels & they run MoEs fine now. But to do this they basically had to turn the routing into dense GEMMs instead, or pad the matrices to fit the MXU dimensions. Which sounds like it would increase the runtime of complexity but it actually doesn’t cause it’s a matrix multiply machine anyway. 

So with that all being said, the fact this team can do higher tokens/sec on Kimi doesn’t surprise me at all. The trade off with Kimi is you get a fixed size KV that doesn’t grow with more context but in return you need to do prefill or checkpoint states more often since you lack precise context. Since decode isn’t bottlenecked by streaming KV cache out of memory every step you can do much bigger batches and serve more users. But the  bottleneck now is redoing prefill which is just dense GEMMs which ofc as you guessed is good for a systolic array… it’s also why Moonshot in their reference design suggests disaggregating prefill and decode to different nodes. 

Long post to say nothing most of you didn’t already know. But the real takeaway to me is it’s looking likely we get a great schism where certain architectures that use hybrid attention will run disproportionately better on stuff like TPUs and other systolic array architectures like Tranium and will cost disproportionately less that many people will make the switch. 

This also leads me to believe that the next Gemini model will likely use a hybrid attention approach and the cost per token and intelligence per token will be much higher.

𝗕𝗶𝘁𝗧𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜𝘁 𝗠𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗧𝗼 𝗕𝗲 𝗔 𝗡𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗨𝘀𝗲𝗿

The traditional internet often separates consumers from the infrastructure delivering their content.

BitTorrent blurs that distinction.

Its peer-to-peer architecture allows users to participate in distribution, turning ordinary devices into additional sources of data.

𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗼 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗿

When a peer downloads pieces of a file, those pieces can also be shared with other participants.

That creates a self-reinforcing network:

More participants → More sources → More available pieces → Greater distribution capacity

Instead of scaling entirely by adding centralized servers, the network can gain capacity through participation.

𝗗𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗔 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿

This model can be useful for large legitimate datasets and digital resources.

Open-source projects can distribute software releases. Researchers can share large datasets. Creators can distribute high-resolution files. Digital archives can maintain multiple copies across participating peers.

The responsibility for delivery does not have to rest entirely on one organization.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲

That is the deeper idea behind BitTorrent.

Users can contribute bandwidth and availability rather than simply consuming a service.

One participant may contribute very little. Millions of participants can create something much larger: a distributed system capable of moving information across geographic boundaries without requiring one central location to handle every transfer.

This principle remains relevant far beyond file sharing.

Decentralized storage, distributed networking, and Web3 infrastructure all explore versions of the same question:

What becomes possible when participants help build the network they use?

BitTorrent has been answering that question for more than two decades.

items.text:
Decentralization Turns File Sharing Into A Network You Don’t Have To Depend On

Centralized platforms made digital storage and sharing incredibly convenient.

But convenience can come with dependency.

A provider can change its pricing, restrict access, throttle bandwidth, discontinue a service, or become unavailable. When one organization controls the infrastructure, users ultimately depend on that organization to keep the system running.

BitTorrent approaches the problem differently.

Instead of putting the entire distribution process behind one provider, it spreads responsibility across participating peers.

Replace The Single Gatekeeper With A Network

Traditional cloud distribution follows a simple model:

Provider stores → Provider serves → Users receive

BitTorrent changes the structure:

Peers share → Peers distribute → The network grows

As participants receive pieces of a file, they can share those pieces with others.

Every active peer can therefore contribute bandwidth and additional distribution capacity.

Decentralization Solves A Real Problem

This isn’t decentralization for the sake of a buzzword.

It can make large-scale distribution more practical.

Developers can distribute substantial software releases.

Researchers can exchange large datasets.

Open-source communities can share resources globally.

Creators can distribute legitimate high-resolution files without placing the entire burden on one centralized server.

The workload becomes collective.

More Participation, More Distribution Capacity

A centralized platform generally needs to increase its infrastructure as demand grows.

If one peer disconnects, the entire system doesn’t necessarily stop.

➠ Additional peers add redundancy to the network.

@soundboy Mostly arithmetic I reckon.

Frontier tokens cost somewhere between 10 and 100x what open or small models charge. 15% of the volume at 30x the price is most of the spend and thats IF it's correct oneshot.

Then the mix. The bulk of tokens are cheap jobs run at huge scale: classification, extraction, summaries, agent sub-steps, synthetic data. Small models do those fine. 

Frontier gets called for the few steps that actually need it, the planning, then judging, and any hard bits. Agents make it more extreme, loads of cheap calls and a handful of expensive ones. Looks at the swarms of hugging face and gulps at the scale of cost there...

And a lot of open source volume is self-hosted, so it counts as tokens but nobody's getting paid for it, and how the devil do we even track true cost there? I don't bloody know!

The case against that pareto distribution being everlasting?  the price gap keeps shrinking, and as it does the split flattens. as said how do we actually track true open source/self hosted tokens at all?

I reckon the shape holds in your example as it stands, but which frontier sits at the top in the next 24 months doesn't.

Like why would a frontier right now with Sam and dario at the helm actually keep the 20%? I don't truly believe it's because they are who they present themselves to be do you?

The split right now comes from how we as users or these LLM value decisions, not from the models at all.
Ease of use and probably branding/word of mouth is the only reason right now we have the 80-20. I guess in this market it will always swing to or lean to that split but in the current form it wont last

Open source and Pliny are making sure obliterated and sef hosting are going to help ( plus Zucks new baby will swallow and probably make it near 50.50 for a while when everyone with Fbook and Insta uses it and falls in love! )

Yourself Ian?

Whats your thoughts on why too? Alays interested in the reason why someone tweets these kind of experiments and what your feel
